accuracy.evidence: Checked against NC Year 2 Living things and their habitats (living, dead, never been alive) and its non-statutory guidance, the PSTT/ASE primary guidance on the three groups and BBC Bitesize KS1 'living and non-living things'. Classifications follow the standard KS1 convention: parts of organisms (bone, shell, feather) and materials from them (wood, paper, wool) are dead/once alive; rock, metal, water and clouds are never alive; dormant seeds, deciduous trees in winter and hibernating hedgehogs are alive. Plastic and coal were deliberately left out because both come from ancient living things and would mislead at this age. The rot scene only claims that once-living material rots and stone does not.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented primary misconceptions on living things (Allen, Misconceptions in Primary Science; Tamir et al. and Bell's 'alive' studies): movement means alive (river, cloud), stillness means dead (seed, bare tree, hibernating hedgehog), made by people means never alive (wooden chair, wool hat), and 'dead' used for never-alive things (a 'dead' stone). Each is a prediction, a wrong-group message or a tagged challenge answer.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagonce is built around the third group: three hoops, a drag-back-to-source scene (chair and paper to a tree, wool to a sheep, a metal spoon to rocks), a three-month time-lapse where only the log grows mushrooms and crumbles, and a signs-of-life check for things that move. flagalive sorts alive/not alive for ages 3–4 with feeding and a robot; it has no once-alive group, no origins and no rotting. Shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Wrong-hoop drops explain the specific reason (a leaf in 'never alive' hears 'It came from something that was alive'); dragging the chair back to the tree makes the 'made but once alive' idea concrete before the text names it; watching the log rot while the stone stays the same gives children a test they can use themselves; tapping 'grows?' for the river shows ✗ before they choose a group.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions with tempting wrong options: a fallen leaf is 'alive now' or 'never alive', a wooden chair is 'no, it is a chair', 'the stone' or 'the tree' will rot, a bare winter tree is 'dead', and a river is 'yes, it moves'. Each is disproved by its task.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating questions with tags made, now, once, move, still and rot; each wrong answer gets a short message naming the slip, e.g. 'People made it, but from wood or wool. That came from something alive.' and 'Being still is not being dead. It is resting and can grow again.'

readability.evidence: Kid text FK grade 1.7 (family target ≤ 5), key idea 4.7, adult 7.2 (≤ 10). Canvas and button words are one or two syllables where possible ('alive now', 'once alive', 'never alive', 'Wait a month'); every card has a large emoji or drawing plus its name, so pre-readers can play with a grown-up reading the step text.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passed with no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with any lesson, including 210 Living and not living and 554 What Living Things Need. Kid paragraphs: the three groups, the signs of life, made things and where they come from, moving and resting. Adult: standard, the rule, four named mistakes, the lab.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 screenshots of every step in dark and light: hoops are a third of the width each with emoji and label legible at 390 px; the card is 140 px wide; the source circles sit below a two-line wrapped feedback note; the rot scene keeps the apples and mushrooms clear of the labels; all buttons use the 56 px young-learner size and wrap two per row.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag and tap has a 56 px labelled button twin: three group buttons with full labels ('The cat is alive now'), three source buttons, Wait a month, the tree/log/stone answers and the three sign checks ('Does the river grow?'). The canvas aria-label repeats every feedback line. walk.cjs: axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
